issues.legal_issue: Temporary administrative arrangements for a religious institution on a disputed succession require an actual vacancy in the office of trustee.
material_facts: An agreement established a procedure for succession and made a governing council the supreme authority on the matter.
A later compromise provided that the respondent would succeed the incumbent as Mahant upon the incumbent’s death.
The governing council approved the respondent’s succession on the day the incumbent died, and the respondent claimed to have assumed the office in his own right.
Other persons disputed the respondent’s succession, and litigation concerning succession was brought.
The administration took charge of the institution under a statutory power for temporary arrangements on the basis that there was a vacancy and a succession dispute.
issues.conclusion: Although a dispute respecting succession existed, there was no vacancy because the respondent had succeeded to the office in his own right; the statutory power to assume temporary management therefore could not be exercised.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 53(1) of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951, the relevant power requires both a vacancy in the office of trustee and a dispute respecting succession. A vacancy means an actual unfilled office: it does not exist where a person with a prima facie legal right has assumed the office. No earlier cases are relied on.

predicates.temporary_management_intervention_case: An administrator seeks to take temporary charge of a religious institution because of a claimed vacancy in its trustee’s office.
predicates.succession_dispute: Two or more people claim the right to succeed to the office of trustee.
predicates.office_occupied_by_person_with_prima_fac: A person with a prima facie legal right to the office has assumed it.

issues.definition: When an administrator seeks temporary charge amid competing succession claims, the stated rule denies jurisdiction if no person with a prima facie legal right has assumed the office.

issues.legal_issue: A trustee who holds office in their own right cannot be suspended under the guise of an interim administrative appointment when the suspension effectively removes the trustee.
material_facts: The respondent had succeeded to the office under the succession arrangements and the governing council’s approval, rather than solely by virtue of the later government appointment.
The government later appointed the respondent as interim Mahant subject to conditions.
The government subsequently placed the respondent under suspension while he claimed to hold the office in his own right.
The suspension effectively removed him from the office of trustee.
issues.conclusion: The government lacked jurisdiction to suspend the respondent under the interim-appointment arrangement because he held the office in his own right and the suspension virtually amounted to removal.
issues.legal_principle: A later government appointment as interim Mahant does not extinguish a trustee’s independent right to hold office. An order suspending such a trustee, when it virtually amounts to removal, can be made only in the manner and circumstances prescribed by section 52 of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951. No earlier cases are relied on.

predicates.government_suspension_case: The government suspends a person who is serving as trustee of a religious institution.
predicates.trustee_holds_office_in_own_right: The trustee’s right to hold office arises independently of a government appointment to serve on an interim basis.
predicates.suspension_operates_as_removal: The suspension effectively removes the trustee from the office.

issues.definition: The rule denies the government authority to suspend a trustee under an interim-appointment power when the trustee holds office independently and the suspension effectively removes the trustee.
